title: Rights and responsibilities
hookLine: God asks Cain a plain question, and Cain answers with a question of his own

cards: A field, just after a killing. God asks Cain a plain question. In the Douay-Rheims: "Where is thy brother Abel?"
Cain tries to slip out the side door: "I know not: am I my brother's keeper?" Underneath the dodge is a whole philosophy. My life is mine.
His is his. What happens to him is none of my business. Catholic social teaching gives Cain an answer he didn't want: yes.
And it builds that answer into the way it talks about rights. Today, rights and responsibilities.

teach.b: First, where rights come from. In Catholic teaching, rights aren't favors a government hands out.
The Catechism says they flow from the dignity of the person and come before society; a society's job is to recognize and protect them.
It names what a truly human life needs: food, clothing, health, work, education, the right to found a family. Second, the pairing. The teaching insists that a right never travels alone.
If I have a right to life, I have a duty to protect life, mine and other people's.

A right to speak brings a duty to tell the truth; a right to a fair wage, a duty of honest work. John the Twenty-Third, in a letter coming later in this block, says rights and duties belong together in the same person.
A right claimed with no duty attached starts to sound like Cain. Third, the size of the duty.
Jesus says in Luke, in the Douay-Rheims: "unto whomsoever much is given, of him much shall be required." More power, money, education or time: more duty. Fourth, the other side of every right.

My right is someone else's duty, and their right is my duty. A child's right to food is a duty for parents, and when parents can't meet it, the duty widens to everyone around them. That's how this week fits together.
It began in Carmel's simple attention, then stepped into the street. Dignity gives every person rights. Family and community are where duties get lived.
And taking part is one of those duties.

how: Catholic teaching presents rights and duties together, and Catholic guides for examining one's conscience include duties toward family, work, neighbors and society, not only private sins.

Church teaching pairs every right with a duty
a right to life brings a duty to protect life; a right to speak, a duty to tell the truth.
"am I my brother's keeper?" is God's question in Genesis
it's Cain's answer, dodging God's question: where is thy brother Abel?

games.q: you're Cain, in the field. God asks: where is thy brother Abel? what do you say?
o: tell the truth and ask for mercy.
"I know not: am I my brother's keeper?"
games.why: Cain dodges with a question. Catholic social teaching gives his question the answer he didn't want: yes.

practice: Let one duty you've been letting slide come to mind, nothing heroic: a call to a parent who's getting older, a form somebody is waiting on, a promise made casually, an apology owed.
Hold it a moment without excuses, then decide when today you'll do it, and picture yourself doing it. If you pray, you can ask God for the nerve.

wordCard.voice: Rights and responsibilities. In Catholic teaching, rights flow from human dignity, and every right comes with a duty, to yourself and to others. Today's word.
